slides.title: Planes inclined to both reference planes
lines: Experiment 10 · CAEG · Semester I 2026–27
Himanshu Giria · PIET, Jaipur

slides.title: Today’s lesson
lines: Construct the manual’s inclined rectangle in stages.
Recover true shape and understand perpendicular distance and the angle between planes.
Complete one AutoCAD drawing and one sketchbook assignment, as specified in the syllabus.

slides.title: A suggested two-hour class
lines: 0–15 min: revision and a card demonstration.
15–55 min: manual rectangle, with students drawing each stage.
55–80 min: true shape, distance and plane angle.
80–110 min: AutoCAD. Last 10 min: checks and viva.

slides.title: The rules from Experiment 9
lines: FV uses height above HP. TV uses depth in front of VP.
Matching views share a projector perpendicular to XY.
A surface parallel to a viewing plane shows true shape. A perpendicular surface shows an edge view.

slides.title: A card you can tilt and turn
lines: Place a rectangular card flat on the desk. Raise it about a short edge.
Keep that edge on the desk and turn the card horizontally.
The tilt to the desk stays the same. Its orientation to the wall changes.

slides.title: The manual rectangle
lines: Rectangle ABCD has AB = 30 mm and AD = 50 mm.
Short side AB rests on HP and makes 30° with VP.
The surface makes 45° with HP. Draw its FV and TV.

slides.title: The two angles describe different things
lines: 45° is the inclination of the entire surface to HP.
30° is the inclination of resting side AB to VP.
AB lies in HP, so its TV shows its true length and true angle to VP.

slides.title: Three positions on the sheet
lines: Position I: surface temporarily in HP. Draw true-shape TV.
Position II: tilt the FV edge view to 45°. Obtain the shortened TV.
Position III: turn that TV until ab is 30° to XY. Transfer heights to obtain final FV.

slides.title: Step 1: the true-shape top view
lines: Draw XY and leave a convenient gap below it.
Draw abcd, 50 mm horizontally and 30 mm vertically. Label in order.
Keep the resting short side ab perpendicular to XY.

slides.title: Step 2: the initial front view
lines: Project each corner up to XY.
a′ and b′ coincide. c′ and d′ coincide.
The FV is a 50 mm line on XY because the temporary surface lies in HP.

slides.title: Step 3: the 45° edge view
lines: In the second position, keep a′b′ on XY.
Draw a 50 mm line at 45° to XY. Its far end is c′d′.
Use the 50 mm span, not the 30 mm resting side.

slides.title: Step 4: the shortened top view
lines: Project down from the tilted FV.
Carry the original depth of each named corner horizontally from Position I.
The intermediate TV is 35.36 mm by 30 mm. Join abcd.

slides.title: Why the 50 mm side becomes shorter
lines: In the tilted FV, the 50 mm span is true length.
Its horizontal component is 50 cos 45° = 35.36 mm.
The raised side is 50 sin 45° = 35.36 mm above HP.

slides.title: Step 5: the resting side at 30°
lines: Copy the whole intermediate TV to Position III.
Turn it until ab makes 30° with XY. Keep the copied shape unchanged.
Do not draw a new 30 × 50 mm rectangle in the final TV.

slides.title: Step 6: the final front-view projectors
lines: Draw projectors upward from final a, b, c and d.
Draw the height loci from the tilted FV: 0 mm and 35.36 mm above XY.
Every final corner must meet its own height locus.

slides.title: Step 7: the final front view
lines: a′ and b′ lie on XY because AB rests on HP.
c′ and d′ lie 35.36 mm above XY.
Join a′b′c′d′a′. Both final views now enclose an area.

slides.title: Step 8: labels and checks
lines: Final TV: ab = 30 mm, ad = 35.36 mm, angle of ab to XY = 30°.
Final FV: resting edge on XY, raised edge 35.36 mm above XY.
Dimension the 45° angle in the intermediate edge view. Keep construction lines thin.

slides.title: The final FV angle can mislead
lines: The surface remains 45° to HP after turning.
The final FV is an area view, so a sloping outline there does not directly give the true surface tilt.
Use the intermediate edge view to show the given 45°.

slides.title: Common construction errors
lines: Tilting a 30 mm line instead of the 50 mm span.
Rotating the original true rectangle instead of the shortened TV.
Transferring depths when the final FV needs heights.
Treating the given 30° side angle as the plane’s inclination to VP.

slides.title: True shape through an auxiliary view
lines: A view taken perpendicular to the surface reveals its true shape.
Start from a view where the surface appears as a line.
For our rectangle, use the intermediate 45° FV edge view.

slides.title: True shape, step 1: a new reference
lines: Draw auxiliary reference X₁Y₁ parallel to the 45° edge view.
Draw auxiliary projectors perpendicular to X₁Y₁ from its endpoint views.
Keep all points on the chosen side of X₁Y₁.

slides.title: True shape, step 2: transfer depths
lines: From the intermediate TV, measure each point’s perpendicular distance from XY.
Transfer these depths from X₁Y₁ on the corresponding auxiliary projectors.
In our chosen layout, A and D have depth 20 mm; B and C have depth 50 mm.

slides.title: True shape, step 3: the rectangle
lines: Join the auxiliary points A₁B₁C₁D₁.
Check AB = 30 mm, AD = 50 mm and all corners = 90°.
The auxiliary view recovers the true shape, independent of the page orientation.

slides.title: Starting from two apparent views
lines: If neither view is an edge view, use two auxiliary stages.
First obtain an edge view. A horizontal line lying in the plane helps choose its viewing direction.
Then use an auxiliary plane parallel to the surface to obtain true shape.
The rectangle already supplies the needed edge view in Position II.

slides.title: Distance of a point from a plane
lines: The distance means the shortest distance, measured along a perpendicular to the plane.
It is not generally the vertical separation in FV.
An auxiliary view showing the plane edge-on and the perpendicular in true length makes it measurable.

slides.title: Distance: a solved teaching example
lines: Plane is perpendicular to VP and has edge view z = x. Point P has x = 20 mm and height z = 50 mm.
Draw P′ = (20, 50). Drop a perpendicular from P′ to the 45° edge line.
Foot N′ = (35, 35). True distance P′N′ = 21.21 mm.

slides.title: Distance: the construction method
lines: 1. Obtain a suitable edge view of the plane and the matching auxiliary view of P.
2. Draw the perpendicular from P to the edge line. Name its foot N.
3. Measure PN there. Transfer N back through projectors if its principal views are required.
Our teaching example uses FV directly because the plane is perpendicular to VP.

slides.title: Angle between two planes
lines: The dihedral angle is measured in a cross-section perpendicular to their line of intersection.
In that view, both planes appear as edge lines.
An arbitrary angle between their outlines in FV or TV can give the wrong answer.

slides.title: Plane angle: a solved teaching example
lines: Two planes are perpendicular to VP and meet along a line perpendicular to VP.
Their FV edge lines make 20° and 65° with XY.
The smaller angle between the planes is 65° − 20° = 45°. The supplementary angle is 135°.

slides.title: Plane angle: the general method
lines: Locate the line where the planes intersect.
Choose an auxiliary viewing direction along that line, making it appear as a point.
Both planes then appear edge-on. Measure the required angle between their edge lines.
Use an intermediate auxiliary view if needed to reach this viewing direction.

slides.title: AutoCAD: preparation
lines: Use a 2D drawing in millimetres, World UCS and a top plan view.
Create separate layers for outline, construction and dimensions.
Use endpoint and intersection object snaps. Turn Dynamic Input off for the coordinate exercise.
The following entries use XY as y = 0 and default counterclockwise angles.

slides.title: AutoCAD 1: initial rectangle
lines: RECTANG: first corner 20,-20; opposite corner 70,-50.
Draw XY with LINE from 0,0 to 300,0. Project x = 20 and x = 70 up to XY.

slides.title: AutoCAD 2: tilted front view
lines: LINE: start 110,0; next point @50<45; Enter to end.
This locates c′d′ at about 145.355,35.355.
Project down and use the y = -20 and y = -50 depth lines from the initial TV.

slides.title: AutoCAD 3: intermediate top view
lines: Use snapped intersections for full precision instead of rounding typed coordinates.
COPY the four TV sides with base point a to a new a at 220,-20.

slides.title: AutoCAD 4: the 30° side angle
lines: ROTATE the copied TV about its new a.
The directed side a to b initially points at 270°. Apply a rotation of -60°.
It now points at 210°, so the undirected resting side makes 30° with XY.

slides.title: AutoCAD 5: the completed FV
lines: Project upward from the final TV vertices.
Intersect a and b projectors with y = 0; c and d projectors with y = 35.355.
Join the final FV. Add labels, DIMALIGNED lengths and DIMANGULAR angles.

slides.title: AutoCAD coordinate check
lines: Final FV uses the same x values: a′, b′ at y = 0 and c′, d′ at y = 35.355.
These rounded values check your construction. Object snaps retain the exact geometry.

slides.title: Sketchbook practice
lines: Teaching assignment: a 30 × 50 mm rectangle rests on its short side on HP.
Surface inclination = 30° to HP. Resting side = 45° to VP.
Draw all three positions, both final views and the true shape. Use your weekly title block.
No submission deadline or marking scheme is set here.

slides.title: Practice checks
lines: Intermediate TV = 43.30 × 30 mm. Raised edge height = 25 mm.
Final TV resting side makes 45° with XY. Final FV resting points remain on XY.
The true shape remains 30 × 50 mm.
Extra: for P′(20,50) and plane edge z = x, confirm 21.21 mm.

slides.title: Viva and quick answers
lines: Why is ab drawn perpendicular to XY initially? To obtain the needed edge view for tilting.
Which length is tilted? The 50 mm span perpendicular to the resting side.
What stays fixed in the final turn? The vertex heights and the intermediate TV shape.
When is a plane’s true shape visible? When the viewing plane is parallel to its surface.

slides.title: Your completed lab record
lines: Aim, given data, instruments or AutoCAD commands, and the stepwise construction.
Three positions with XY, point labels, light projectors and the specified dimensions.
Result: final projections satisfy the surface and resting-side conditions.
Include the AutoCAD drawing and sketchbook assignment specified in Chapter X.
